name: Bayungu
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 9 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Austin, Peter K. & Alan Dench. 2018 (page published 2018-07-31, modified 2024-08-05). 'Spelling'. Languages of the Gascoyne Region, Western Australia (website, 'This website was created by Peter K. Austin and Alan Dench').https://yinggarda.org/welcome-to-the-yinggarda-language/spelling/(accessed 2026-09-17).
catalog_locator: Spelling page, last two paragraphs of the pronunciation guide (unpaginated web page); the guide covers the site's three languages Yinggarda, Bayungu and Burduna and names Bayungu explicitly.
catalog_quote: Words in Gascoyne region Indigenous languages must end in a vowel, and words begin with one and only one consonant. ... In general, stress (emphasis) falls on the first vowel of a word. So, for example, the name of the language Yinggarda is pronounced as ying-ga-rda with stress on the ying. Do not put emphasis on later syllables as this sounds very unnatural in Yinggarda (English speakers might be tempted to say ying-ga–rda with stress on the middle syllable this would sound very strange to Yinggarda people). The same is true of Bayungu (pronounced ba-yoo-ngoo not ba-yoo-ngoo) and other languages.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (title 'Spelling - Languages of the Gascoyne Region, Western Australia'; og meta published 2018-07-31, modified 2024-08-05). The quoted passage is the final paragraph of the entry content and matches word for word: 'Words in Gascoyne region Indigenous languages must end in a vowel, and words begin with one and only one consonant. [elided sentence about y/w lightly sounded] In general, stress (emphasis) falls on the first vowel of a word. So, for example, the name of the language Yinggarda is pronounced as ying-ga-rda with stress on the ying. Do not put emphasis on later syllables.. The same is true of Bayungu (pronounced ba-yoo-ngoo not ba-yoo-ngoo) and other languages.' Raw HTML car…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress falls on the first syllable (first vowel) of the word; the language name Bayungu is stressed BA-yu-ngu, and stressing a later syllable is wrong. Independently, Goedemans 1998 (StressTyp, Appendix D) classes Payungu as 'Initial main stress, no info on secondary stress' on the basis of Austin 1992.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said on the web page; Goedemans 1998 explicitly files Payungu under 'no info on sec stress'.
new_statements.exceptions: None ('In general' is the only hedge).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level, citation-form pronunciation guidance in a practical orthography guide; no discussion of clitics, compounds or phrase-level prominence.
new_statements.identity_note: The statement is made for the shared Gascoyne-region orthography (Yinggarda, Bayungu, Burduna) and then explicitly extended to Bayungu by name with the example BA-yu-ngu; Bayungu = Payungu (Austin's earlier spelling), Glottolog bayu1240, ISO bxj. Goedemans 1998 lists it as 'Payungu (T70)' (Tindale number).

sources.citation: Austin, Peter. 1981. Proto-Kanyara and proto-Mantharta historical phonology. Lingua 54: 295-333.http://peterkaustin.com/docs/Austin_1981_Lingua.pdf
sources.note: Segmental historical phonology only (nasal loss/stopping, stop voicing, lenition); the words 'stress' and 'accent' do not occur anywhere in the paper.

sources.citation: O'Grady, G.N. 1979. Preliminaries to a Proto Nuclear Pama-Nyungan stem list. In S.A. Wurm (ed.), Australian Linguistic Studies (Pacific Linguistics C-54), 107-139.http://sealang.net/archives/pl/pdf/PL-C54.107.pdf
sources.note: 'All words were stressed on the first syllable' is asserted of reconstructed Proto Nuclear Pama-Nyungan (pp.131-2), not of Bayungu; Bayungu appears only as a cognate witness.

sources.citation: Walsh, Michael (2010). Introduction: Language centres and programs. In Re-awakening languages: theory and practice in the revitalisation of Australia's Indigenous languages. Sydney University Press. pp. 103-105.

sources.note: The only Bayungu content is p. 104: 'they present five case studies involving different languages: Thalanyji, Ngarluma, Nyangumarta and Bayungu as well as a group of eight Pilbara languages' and 'The fifth is a Bayungu picture dictionary in which a template for another dictionary is recycled'. Nothing on word stress, so it neither supports nor contradicts the catalog's initial-stress record. Glottolog's 'grammar sketch' kind for this item is wrong: it is a revitalisation-programme editorial, not a description of the language.
